prompt.context: Bob is a master brewer and has been brewing beer for the past decade. Upon graduating from Stern, he opened a brewery on the Upper West Side called Something Witty that features Belgian Witbier styled brews. While he found early success, he has noticed an increase in customers asking for gluten-free alternatives, such as cider. Bob has hired us to help him analyze his options.
prompt.question: Bob has decided to explore expansion into cider. How should he think about this decision, and what would you recommend?

clarifying_info.a: Bob's goal is to continue to be profitable regardless of what expansion opportunity he explores.

clarifying_info.q: What does Bob currently sell and how?
clarifying_info.a: Currently, Bob only sells bottled beer direct to consumers.

clarifying_info.q: How many bottles are in a case?
How many days per month does production run?
clarifying_info.a: Production runs Monday through Friday — assume 20 days per month.

clarifying_info.q: How much cider is sold in NYC annually?
clarifying_info.a: 15.5 million bottles of cider are expected to be sold in New York City next year.

exhibits.title: Bottled Beverage Production
exhibits.shows: A table comparing beer and cider production volumes and selling prices under two scenarios: Current State and After Renovations for Cider Production.

framework: Alternatives to cider entry: other drinks (wine, cocktails), experiences (live music, themed nights), food menu additions
Products/Renovations: equipment needs, licensing, break-even point
Market assessment: market size, competitors, customer tastes and preferences, cannibalization risk
Capabilities: organic/in-house production vs. outsourcing, equipment, training, ingredients, sufficient space, current capacity utilization

questions.prompt: Question 1a: Bob has created Exhibit 1 detailing impacts to current production if he undergoes renovations to accommodate cider production. What are your thoughts on the two options (Current State vs. After Renovations)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize pros and cons of each option and identify that other expansion paths exist beyond renovating the existing factory (e.g., building a new facility, buying cider from an existing manufacturer and reselling). Current State pros: specialization in one product, consistent marketing message, specialized labor. Current State cons: not meeting demand for gluten-free customers, not increasing revenue potential. After Renovations pros: new product offering, cider has a higher selling price than beer. After Renovations cons: beer production decreases by 6 cases/day, upfront renovation costs.

questions.prompt: Question 1b: What will be the change in Bob's annual revenue if he begins to produce cider?
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate annual revenue in the Current State vs. After Renovations and find the difference. Strong candidates will recognize the shortcut: calculate the revenue change directly (lost beer revenue + new cider revenue).

math.setup: Production days = 20 days/month × 12 months = 240 days/year. Bottles per case = 30. Current annual beer revenue = 30 cases × 30 bottles × $5.00 × 240 days. Post-renovation beer revenue = 24 cases × 30 bottles × $5.00 × 240 days. Post-renovation cider revenue = 12 cases × 30 bottles × $6.00 × 240 days.

questions.prompt: Question 2: Besides potential revenue, what other factors should Bob consider before expanding into the cider market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should quickly identify cost as a key factor, then brainstorm broadly across the categories below.

questions.prompt: Question 3: Bob has determined that he needs to capture at least 0.5% of the NYC take-home cider market annually in order to break even. Will he be able to produce enough cider to capture 0.5%?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use (or be given) the result from Q1b: Bob produces 86,400 bottles of cider per year. Compare this to 0.5% of the NYC market. Since 86,400 > 77,500, Bob can produce enough. An excellent candidate will also note that production capacity is necessary but not sufficient — Bob still needs to actually sell that volume.

math.setup: Bob's annual cider production = 12 cases/day × 30 bottles × 240 days/year. NYC market 0.5% threshold = 15,500,000 bottles × 0.5%.
steps: 86,400 > 77,500 → Bob can produce enough to meet the break-even threshold
math.answer: Yes, Bob can produce 86,400 bottles/year, which exceeds the 77,500-bottle break-even threshold (0.5% of the 15.5M-bottle NYC market).

brainstorming.prompt: Besides potential revenue, what other factors should Bob consider before expanding into the cider market?

categories.name: Cost
ideas: Raw materials (apples and other cider ingredients)

categories.name: Market Size and Demand
ideas: Relative size of cider vs. beer market
Number of new customers cider would attract
Growth rate of cider vs. beer markets

categories.name: Impact on Core Business
ideas: Effect on brand equity and brand identity

recommendation: Bob should make the investment to produce cider. He will see an increase in annual revenues of $302,400 and can produce 86,400 bottles per year, which exceeds the 77,500-bottle break-even threshold (0.5% of the NYC market).
risks: Uncertain trajectory of the cider market — can Bob reliably meet demand over time?
Cannibalization of existing beer products and loyal beer customers
Competitive intensity in the cider industry
Demand risk: production capacity does not guarantee sales — Bob has not yet validated that he can sell 77,500+ bottles annually
next_steps: Conduct a competitive analysis of the NYC cider market
Pressure-test Bob's 0.5% break-even assumption with sensitivity analysis
Commission market research to identify the optimal price point, flavor profile, and packaging that will resonate with target customers
